# 26 Testing for Backend Engineers

Part of [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/Backend from First Principles|Backend from First Principles]] · Previous: [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/25 Real-Time Backends/25 Real-Time Backends|25 Real-Time Backends]] · Next: [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/27 The Twelve-Factor App/27 The Twelve-Factor App|27 The Twelve-Factor App]]

This lesson covers the testing a **backend engineer writes and runs themselves**, which is most of the testing in a typical team. It explains what a test really is, the kinds of tests and a practical way to classify them, **test doubles** (mocks, stubs, fakes…), how to make code **testable**, how to deal with **databases, networks and time**, **TDD**, **flaky tests**, how to measure a test suite (**coverage**, **mutation testing**), and how to measure code (**cyclomatic and cognitive complexity**, linters and static analysis).

Manual QA processes, test-management tools, mobile testing and browser automation for frontends are **out of scope**.

---

## 1. Why testing comes last in this series

Across more than 20 lessons, no tests were written, **on purpose**. A **bad, rushed or incomplete test is worse than no test**, because it gives **false confidence** in your code. Instead of squeezing a small testing section into every lesson, testing gets a full lesson of its own.

### The example codebase

The tests in this lesson are written for the **task board** from [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/25 Real-Time Backends/25 Real-Time Backends|lesson 25]], a Go project of about 11 files:

| Path | Role |
|---|---|
| `cmd/board` | The executable. `main` is the **only place that wires everything together**. |
| `internal/board` | The domain: tasks, columns, moving tasks |
| `internal/hub` | "Rooms" for boards; each subscriber in a room has its own counter |
| `internal/bus` | An **interface with two methods** and **two implementations**: an **in-process** one (used in tests) and a **Redis** one (used in production) |
| `internal/store` | An **interface with three methods**, backed by **PostgreSQL** |
| `internal/httpapi` | The **route table**: one file showing every endpoint |

Having the same interface with a test implementation and a production implementation is one of the core uses of **interfaces**. You don't need to know Go: the ideas carry over to any language, and the code only makes them concrete.

---

## 2. What a test is

> A **test** is a **second program** that **runs your program** and **makes claims** about what happened.

It calls your code with **inputs you chose in advance**, looks at the **output**, and **complains** (fails, errors, panics) if the output isn't what you expected.

Even with **no testing tools at all**, this is a test:

```go
// Illustrative: a "test" with no framework at all
func checkTotal() {
    if got := Total([]int{5, 15}); got != 20 {
        panic(fmt.Sprintf("Total = %d, want 20", got))
    }
}
```

Hand-writing every check, test runner and mock doesn't scale for complex applications, so languages ship testing support and libraries build nicer tools on top. Every test type, metric and tool in this lesson is a **variation of this definition**.

### Why write tests?

- **Guidance**: in **test-driven development (TDD)** you write the test first so the goal is clear (section 21).
- **Documentation**: tests show how code is meant to be used.
- **Most importantly: catching regressions** (section 5).

---

## 3. Test runners

A **test runner** is a program that **finds all your tests**, **runs them**, and reports **how many passed and failed**.

The first test for the board creates a board, **moves a task** to another column, and checks the task ended up where expected:

```go
// Illustrative Go test
func TestMoveTask(t *testing.T) {
    b := board.New()
    task := b.AddTask("Write notes", board.Todo)

    if err := b.Move(task.ID, board.Doing); err != nil {
        t.Fatalf("Move returned error: %v", err)
    }
    if got := b.Task(task.ID).Column; got != board.Doing {
        t.Errorf("task column = %q, want %q", got, board.Doing)
    }
}
```

**Demo (shown in the lesson):**

- **A deliberate failure:** with a wrong expectation, the output showed the **file, the line number, and want vs got** (the task was in `doing`, the test wanted `done`). After fixing the expectation, the test passed instantly.
- **Keeping the build folder:** `go test -work` keeps the build folder and prints its path. Inside was a generated file, **`_testmain.go`**, which the tool wrote, not the developer. It declares `package main`, holds a **list of every test function** found in the package, and has a `func main` that calls `testing.MainStart` and then `os.Exit`.
- **Seeing every command:** `go test -x` prints every command the tool runs. The last ones **link a binary called `board.test`** and **run it**.

So `go test` **writes a `main` function, compiles it into a program, and executes it**. In any language, the runner's job is the same: generate the entry point you'd otherwise write yourself, and **collect the results**.

---

## 4. Assertions and failure messages

An **assertion** is a check that **fails or stops the test** when a condition isn't true.

- Most languages use an assertion library with helpers like `assertEquals`, `assertNotEquals` and so on.
- Go's standard library has **no assert function**. You write a plain `if` and call **`t.Errorf`** (record a failure and continue) or `t.Fatalf` (record a failure and stop this test), with your own message.

**Always write a meaningful failure message**: what was checked, what was expected, what actually happened. Whoever sees the failure should know where to look without re-reading the whole test.

---

## 5. Regressions and CI

A **regression** is a bug you **already fixed that comes back**, or a feature that **used to work and breaks**. It typically happens when someone changes a function, interface or behaviour, which is normal in a team.

Tests catch regressions **immediately** when they run in **CI** (continuous integration, e.g. **GitHub Actions**):

1. Someone opens a pull request.
2. CI runs the **whole test suite** before the code can merge into `main` or `develop`.
3. If a test fails, you know **this change** brings back an old bug, and you fix it **before users notice**.

A reliable, **deterministic** test suite that covers past bugs lets a team **move fast** without fear of breaking existing features.

---

## 6. Unit, integration and end-to-end tests

### Unit test

A **unit test** tests **one unit of code in isolation**. But what is a "unit": a function, a struct, a package, a service? **There's no universal definition.** You learn to recognise it with experience.

If a function calls two or three others, you can either let it call the **real** ones or pass in **mocks**. Both are commonly called unit tests.

### Integration test

An **integration test** checks **two or more parts working together**. Usually one part is your code and the other is something **external you didn't write**, such as a **database**.

### End-to-end (E2E) test

An **end-to-end test** goes through the **whole system the way a real user would**: **log in** first, keep the session or token, then open the dashboard, call APIs, create a task, and so on, following a **user journey**.

The difference from integration tests: an **integration test** can use internal shortcuts, e.g. create a task directly and **skip authentication**. An **E2E test** must follow every step a real user takes.

---

## 7. What makes a test slow: leaving the process

**Demo (shown in the lesson):** the **same behaviour** (moving a task) tested four ways:

| # | What it used | Time |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | A **mock bus** that only records what it was asked to publish | ~0 s |
| 2 | The **real bus and real hub**; the move reaches a real subscriber | ~0 s |
| 3 | A **real HTTP server** on a real port, a real POST, the real response read back | ~0 s |
| 4 | A **real PostgreSQL** database | **~10.5 s**, mostly the **Postgres container booting** |

The lesson: test cost isn't driven by **how much logic** a test covers. The full HTTP stack still took about zero time. It's driven by whether the test **leaves its own process** for external territory.

---

## 8. The test pyramid

The well-known **test pyramid**:

```text
        /  E2E  \          few: slow, expensive
       /---------\
      / integration\       some
     /-------------\
    /     unit      \      many: fast, cheap
```

The pyramid is about **cost**. The higher a test sits, the **slower and more expensive** it is: not necessarily money, but **CPU, memory and time**. So write **many cheap tests** and **few expensive ones**.

---

## 9. A more practical model: what a test may touch

Instead of asking *"how much of the system does this test cover?"*, ask: **"What is this test allowed to touch?"** (the creator's preferred model):

| Size | Allowed to touch |
|---|---|
| **Small** | **One process only**: no network, no database, no file system, no sleeping |
| **Medium** | Things **on the same machine**, e.g. a Postgres or Redis container running locally, but **no internet** |
| **Large** | **Anything** |

Why this is better:

- **Nobody can objectively check** whether something is "really" a unit test, because there's no agreed definition. A machine **can** check whether a test **opened a socket**, so size is a rule you can **enforce**, not an argument.
- It **reduces flakiness**. A **flaky test** passes sometimes and fails other times on the same code. Most flakiness comes from the **outside world** (external services, network, other machines' clocks). Keeping tests inside the process or machine pushes **determinism** to its maximum.

Unit, integration and E2E answer "how much does it touch?". That's **scope**, and in this model scope is: **in the process, on the machine, or beyond**.

---

## 10. Other names for tests

Other test names describe a test's **purpose**, not a new scope. Each can be small, medium or large.

| Name | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Regression test** | Prevents a **specific past bug** from returning |
| **Functional test** | Checks the system does what its **specification** requires (closely related to the TDD idea of writing the spec as a test) |
| **Performance test** | Measures **speed**, plus **memory and CPU** usage |
| **Security test** | Checks for security and privacy weaknesses: bypassed access controls, insecure cookies, files or data exposed |

A regression test can be a unit test, and a security test can be an E2E test. Industry still uses these words, so it's worth knowing them, but the creator thinks in terms of **what a test touches**.

---

## 11. Why code is hard to test

Why don't more people write tests? Consider the board's **move handler**:

1. It asks the board to apply the change.
2. It **publishes an event on the bus**, so other browsers see it (lesson 25).

In a real backend it might also **write to Postgres**, **call a payment provider** to check credits, and **send an email**. How do you test that workflow without a real database, a real payment and a real email?

**Answer:** give the code something that **looks and acts like** the external service. That stand-in is a **test double**, named after **stunt doubles** in films, who do the risky scenes while viewers believe it's the actor.

---

## 12. Test doubles: dummy, stub, spy, mock, fake

"Test double" is the category name. There are **five kinds**, though people often call all of them "mocks":

| Kind | What it does | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Dummy** | Passed in only because the function signature **requires it**; **never actually used** | A do-nothing logger handed to a constructor in a test that doesn't care about logs |
| **Stub** | Returns **pre-written (canned) answers** | "Get user 7" always returns the same user object, so the code under test isn't blocked waiting on a real user |
| **Spy** | A stub that also **records how it was used** | Returns user 7, **and** records that you asked to rename the user from X to Y |
| **Mock** | Pre-programmed with **expectations**; **fails the test** if they're not met | "`Save` must be called **exactly once** with this argument" |
| **Fake** | A **working but simplified implementation**, not fit for production, that **behaves like the real thing** | A user store that saves users in an **in-memory map** instead of Postgres; you can save and read back |

```go
// Illustrative: a fake bus (in-memory) and a spy-like recorder
type RecordingBus struct {
    Published []Event
}

func (b *RecordingBus) Publish(ctx context.Context, topic string, e Event) error {
    b.Published = append(b.Published, e) // records instead of sending to Redis
    return nil
}
```

---

## 13. State verification vs interaction verification

There are two ways to write the final check of a move-handler test:

| Approach | What it asks | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **State verification** | What **state** is the system in now? | Is the task in the `done` column? Did the sequence number go up by one? |
| **Interaction (behaviour) verification** | What did the **double observe**? | Was `Publish` called **once** with an event of type `task.moved`? |

Now suppose someone changes the code so the handler publishes **one combined event instead of two**. From the outside **nothing changed**: every browser shows the same board.

- The **state** test still passes, correctly.
- The **interaction** test **fails**, because the number of calls changed.

A test that breaks when the **implementation** changes even though **behaviour** didn't is a **change-detector test** (Google's testing blog has a well-known post on this). It adds maintenance cost without catching real bugs.

**Rule of thumb:** assert **what the system is now**, not **how it got there**. Use interaction verification **only when the interaction itself matters**, e.g. an email must be sent **exactly once**.

---

## 14. Don't mock what you don't own

Your service calls a **payment provider**, and you don't want to charge a real card many times a day. So you mock their client: "when `Charge` is called with these arguments, return a success object with `data`, `success`, `newBalance`." The tests pass, you deploy, and **production fails**.

Why? **Everything the test checked, you wrote yourself**: the response shape, the field names, the duplicate-charge behaviour, the error formats. The mock only confirmed your own assumptions.

**Rule: don't mock what you don't own.** Instead:

1. **Wrap the third party in your own small interface** that uses **your** types: your success and failure objects, your errors. Use the wrapper in production **and** in tests. Since you own this interface, you may fake it.
2. **Write a few contract tests against the provider's sandbox** (most payment providers offer one). They check that your wrapper's assumptions about requests, responses, successes and failures **match the real API**. They're quick and involve no real payments.

```go
// Illustrative: your own interface around a payment provider
type Payments interface {
    Charge(ctx context.Context, userID string, cents int64) (ChargeResult, error)
}
// prod:  stripePayments{...}  (adapts the provider's SDK to this interface)
// tests: fakePayments{...}    (in-memory)
```

---

## 15. Dependency injection

The move handler was hard to test because it **created its own dependencies**: it built the database client and the Redis client and connected them itself. A function that **creates what it depends on** gives callers **no way to replace** those dependencies.

**Dependency injection (DI):** **pass dependencies in** (as parameters or constructor arguments) instead of creating them inside.

```go
// Illustrative
// Hard to test: creates its own dependencies
func NewHandler() *Handler {
    db := postgres.MustConnect(os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL"))
    rdb := redis.NewClient(&redis.Options{Addr: "localhost:6379"})
    return &Handler{store: db, bus: redisbus.New(rdb)}
}

// Testable: dependencies are injected
func NewHandler(store Store, bus Bus) *Handler {
    return &Handler{store: store, bus: bus}
}
// main wires the real Postgres and Redis; tests pass fakes.
```

DI frameworks exist and can help as a codebase grows, but they all do this same thing. (This builds on the layering in [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/10 Controllers, Services, Repositories, Middlewares and Request Context/10 Controllers, Services, Repositories, Middlewares and Request Context|lesson 10]].)

---

## 16. Functional core, imperative shell

A useful design for testability:

- **Functional core:** put decisions, calculations and business rules into **pure functions**. They **take values and return values**, with no side effects.
- **Imperative shell:** keep everything that **talks to the outside world** (databases, APIs, providers, email) in a **thin layer** around the core.

```text
┌──────────────── imperative shell (thin) ────────────────┐
│ HTTP handler → load from DB → CORE → save → publish     │
│                        ┌──────────────┐                 │
│                        │ pure logic   │ ← easy to test  │
│                        └──────────────┘                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

- The **core** is **easy to test**: nothing to mock, and you own all of it.
- The **shell** is harder to test, but it's **so thin there's little to test**.

Structured this way, you're much more likely to actually write tests.

---

## 17. Databases: test against the real thing

### The tempting shortcut

"The database is slow, so replace it in tests with something **in memory**": hand-written fake repositories in Go, in-memory replacements in Node.js, **H2** in Java. You gain **speed** and convenience. You lose **fidelity** (how faithfully the test matches reality).

Think about the bugs that live in the data layer:

- a **wrong column name**,
- a **missing index** that makes a query slow,
- a **unique constraint** you forgot to handle,
- a **transaction** that doesn't do what you think,
- a **JSON operator** that exists in Postgres but not in your fake (or the other way round).

All of those bugs live in **exactly the layer you replaced**.

**Solution: test against a real database, and make it cheap.**

### Technique 1: a transaction per test

1. At the start of the test, **open a transaction**.
2. Run everything inside it.
3. At the end, **roll back** instead of committing.

The database is untouched, so the next test starts from a **clean slate**, and it's **fast**. **Requirement:** the code under test must accept a **transaction handle** instead of a database handle, which is easy with dependency injection.

```go
// Illustrative
func TestCreateTask(t *testing.T) {
    tx, err := testDB.BeginTx(ctx, nil)
    if err != nil { t.Fatal(err) }
    t.Cleanup(func() { tx.Rollback() }) // undo everything this test did

    repo := store.New(tx) // the repository accepts a tx (DI)
    ...
}
```

### Technique 2: a template database

PostgreSQL can **create a database as a copy of another**:

1. Run all **migrations** once on a **template** database (see [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/12 Databases with Postgres/12 Databases with Postgres#9. Migrations|lesson 12]]).
2. Each test creates **its own database from the template** in milliseconds:

```sql
-- Illustrative
CREATE DATABASE test_7f3a TEMPLATE app_template;
```

Each test has its own database, so tests can also **run in parallel**.

### Testcontainers

**Testcontainers** is a library with SDKs for most languages. It **starts a real container** (Postgres or many other databases) **from your test code** and gives you its address.

**Demo (shown in the lesson):**

- **Startup:** Testcontainers started a real **PostgreSQL 18** container and waited until it accepted connections. It was ready about **7 seconds** later, **once for the whole package**, not per test.
- **The tests:** each of the **nine tests** created its own database from the template and ran in **milliseconds**.
- **Total:** about **10.5 s** for the whole package, roughly 7 s of setup plus 3 s of actual tests.

---

## 18. Network: real HTTP in tests

When your code calls **someone else's API**:

1. **Wrap it in your own interface** and fake that (section 14).
2. When you need to test the **HTTP client code itself** (headers, request building, error handling), start a **real HTTP server inside the test** and point your client at it:
   - Go: **`net/http/httptest`**,
   - Node.js and Python have well-maintained equivalents,
   - **MSW** (Mock Service Worker) for Node intercepts requests **at the network layer**, so you don't have to swap your client.

The request travels over **real TCP**, as in production. The same approach lets you test **your own handlers from the outside**.

```go
// Illustrative
srv := httptest.NewServer(http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    w.Write([]byte(`{"status":"ok"}`))
}))
defer srv.Close()

client := weather.NewClient(srv.URL) // your client, pointed at the test server
```

---

## 19. Time: stop sleeping

A common pattern: call something that does work **in the background**, then **sleep 100 ms** before checking the result. It passes on your laptop and in review, then **fails in CI**: the CI machine was busy and the work took **110 ms**.

Your logic wasn't wrong; **the clock was**. Increasing the sleep is a naive fix: a busier day breaks it again, and every increase makes the suite slower.

### Fix 1: wait for a condition, not a duration

Wait for a **signal** that the work is done: in Go, a value on a **channel**; in Node.js, a **callback** or promise resolving.

```go
// Illustrative
done := make(chan struct{})
worker.OnFinished(func() { close(done) })
worker.Start()

select {
case <-done: // proceed as soon as it's actually finished
case <-time.After(5 * time.Second):
    t.Fatal("worker did not finish") // generous upper bound, rarely reached
}
```

### Fix 2: inject the clock

Pass a **clock** into your code instead of letting it read real time. In tests, use a **fake clock** you control, so you can "advance time" instantly and test timeouts deterministically. Many languages and libraries support this.

```go
// Illustrative
type Clock interface{ Now() time.Time }
// prod: realClock{}   tests: &fakeClock{t: fixedTime}  (advance manually)
```

---

## 20. Hermetic tests

A **hermetic** test (hermetic means **sealed**) **brings its own environment**. It doesn't depend on a database someone set up by hand or a service that happens to be running. **Everything it needs, it starts; when it's done, it stops everything it started.**

That's what lets tests run **anywhere**: your laptop, a remote server, GitHub Actions.

- **Testcontainers** makes a test hermetic about the **database**.
- An **injected clock** makes it hermetic about **time**.

---

## 21. Test-driven development: red, green, refactor

**Test-driven development (TDD)** is a **way of working**, not a type of test: you write the test (the specification) **before** the code. The tests themselves are still ordinary small, medium or large tests.

### The loop

| Phase | What you do | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| 🔴 **Red** | Write a test for something that **doesn't exist yet**; run it and watch it **fail** | **Design**: you use the function before it exists, so you design its **API from the caller's side**. If the test is awkward to write, the interface is wrong, and you find out in minutes, not at the end. |
| 🟢 **Green** | Write the **smallest** amount of code that makes it pass; ugly code is allowed | **Proof**: seeing red turn green shows the test really checks something. A test written after the code usually passes first time, which proves nothing. |
| 🔵 **Refactor** | Clean up, run the tests again; they should **stay green** | **Quality**: the step most people **skip**, but it's mandatory. Ugly code was only allowed in green *because* you come back here. |

Seeing a test fail before it passes is one of the properties Kent Beck, the originator of TDD, lists as desirable in a test.

---

## 22. A TDD example

**Requirement:** a task **can't jump straight from To do to Done**; it must pass through **Doing** first. No code enforces this yet.

**Red:** a test takes a task in `todo`, moves it to `done`, and **expects an error**. It fails: it expected an error but got `nil`, because the move succeeded.

```go
// Illustrative
func TestCannotSkipDoing(t *testing.T) {
    b := board.New()
    task := b.AddTask("Ship it", board.Todo)

    if err := b.Move(task.ID, board.Done); err == nil {
        t.Fatal("moving todo → done should fail, got nil error")
    }
}
```

**Green:** add **one `if` statement** inside `Move`. The test passes.

**Refactor:** that `if` is a **business rule** sitting in a method that also locks a mutex, increments a sequence number and trims a history buffer. Extract it into a pure function:

```go
// Illustrative
func canMove(from, to Column) bool {
    return !(from == Todo && to == Done)
}
```

Run the whole package again: **still green**. The code improved and the behaviour is protected. The loop is complete.

---

## 23. The TDD debate, and when TDD fits

TDD is heavily debated. Some reading:

- **Kent Beck (2023)** wrote a short article ("Canon TDD") describing what the loop actually means.
- **Ian Cooper, "TDD, Where Did It All Go Wrong"**: people took "unit" to mean **a class**, wrote one test class per production class and **mocked everything else**, so every refactor broke hundreds of tests and many gave up on TDD. His point: the **unit is a behaviour**, tested through a module's **public interface**. Then you can rearrange the internals freely and the tests still pass. This matches section 13: test **outcomes**, not **implementation**.
- **DHH** (creator of Ruby on Rails), **"TDD is dead. Long live testing." (2014)**: argued against test-first dogma and designing systems around **mockability**, in favour of testing against real things. It led to public discussions between DHH, **Kent Beck** and **Martin Fowler** ("Is TDD Dead?").

### The creator's view

- **TDD fits** when you **know what the answer should look like** but not **how to build it**: e.g. a **parser** (input string → expected structure), a **pricing rule**, a **state machine**. Writing expectations is the easy part, and TDD keeps you focused.
- **TDD fits poorly** when you're still **exploring**: trying approaches, weighing trade-offs, discovering what feels right. In the creator's experience much backend feature work is like this, so TDD is useful but not for everything.

---

## 24. Flaky tests

A **flaky test** **passes and fails on the same code**, without any change.

### Why it's worse than no test

- A **missing** test is an **honest gap**: you know there's a hole.
- A **flaky** test **changes team behaviour**. CI fails, someone says "that one's flaky, just re-run it", it passes, and everyone moves on. Eventually a **real** failure appears, and the first reaction is to **re-run** it instead of fixing it.

### Where flakiness comes from

A **2014 study by Luo et al.** analysed **201 real fixes** of flaky tests in open-source projects and grouped them by cause. The top three:

| Cause | Meaning | Fix in this lesson |
|---|---|---|
| **Async wait** | The test starts something and **waits for it the wrong way** | Wait for a **condition**, not a duration (section 19) |
| **Concurrency** | Two things in the test **race** each other (see [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/22 Concurrency and Parallelism/22 Concurrency and Parallelism#12. The danger: shared state and race conditions|lesson 22]]) | Synchronisation primitives; in Go, **`testing/synctest`** |
| **Test-order dependency** | Test B passes **only if test A ran first** and left state behind (a DB row, a global variable, a file) | Make each test set up its own state (hermetic, transaction per test) |

Order dependency is dangerous because the suite passes as long as the order never changes. Then someone **adds a test in the middle** or turns on **parallelism**, and it breaks.

### What to do with a flaky test

1. **Delete it.** It wasn't helping much and will cause future problems. Deleting tests pays off more often than people expect.
2. **Quarantine it** (the creator's preferred option): move it out of the **blocking** suite into a separate one that still runs, labelled with **an owner's name, a date and the reason**. When it misbehaves, you know whom to ask.
3. **Add automatic retries.** Possible, but **not good practice**: it hides the problem.

## 25. Code coverage

**Code coverage** is the **percentage of your code executed while the tests ran**.

### How it's measured

When you ask for coverage, the tool **rewrites your code before building it**:

1. It splits each function into **basic blocks**, straight runs of code with no branches.
2. It inserts a **counter** at the start of each block.
3. It runs the tests and reads the counters. A block with **count 0 never ran**.

### Coverage only tracks execution

Coverage records that code **ran**, not that anything **checked** it. A test that calls every function and **asserts nothing** can reach **100%**.

### Different kinds of coverage

| Kind | Measures |
|---|---|
| **Line (statement) coverage** | Did each line run? |
| **Branch coverage** | Did each **direction** of each decision (true **and** false) happen? |

```go
// Illustrative
func discount(price int, member bool) int {
    if member {
        price = price * 90 / 100
    }
    return price
}
// One test with member = true: line coverage 100%, branch coverage 50%
// (the "member = false" direction was never taken)
```

---

## 26. Does coverage measure quality?

**80%** is a commonly quoted target. Does higher coverage mean better tests?

**Inozemtseva and Holmes (ICSE 2014)** generated **thousands of test suites** of different sizes for large real-world **Java** programs, measured each suite's coverage, and counted how many **faults** each one caught.

- Naively correlating coverage with faults found shows a **strong** relationship, but mostly because **bigger suites** both cover more and find more.
- **Controlling for suite size** (comparing suites of the **same size**) leaves only a **low to moderate** correlation between coverage and effectiveness, varying between programs.

So **a fixed coverage target doesn't produce an effective test suite**.

### How to use coverage sensibly

These guidelines come from Google's published coverage best practices:

1. **Rough levels:** **60% acceptable, 75% commendable, 90% exemplary**, with **no single ideal number** for every product.
2. **What's *not* covered matters more than the percentage.** The value of a coverage report is in its **red (uncovered) lines**.
3. **Don't make 100% mandatory.** People will write **low-value tests** just to hit the number, then **stop improving** once they reach it.

A more useful direction is **mutation testing**.

---

## 27. Mutation testing: testing your tests

**Mutation testing** deliberately **breaks your code** and checks whether your tests **notice**.

1. The tool makes many **small changes** to your source, one at a time:
   - `>` → `>=`,
   - `+` → `-`,
   - replace a return value with `0`.

   Each changed version is a **mutant**.
2. It runs your test suite against each mutant:
   - a test **fails** → the mutant is **killed** ✅ (your tests caught the damage),
   - all tests **pass** → the mutant **survived** ❌ (your tests didn't really check that code).
3. **Mutation score** = percentage of mutants killed.

**Demo (shown in the lesson):** a module that takes a list and returns **one page** of it. Its tests asserted weak things: "returns something", "returns an array", "doesn't throw", "length > 0".

- **Coverage:** 100% of lines.
- **Mutation testing** with **Stryker**: 19 mutants, score **52.63%**, so **9 survived**.
- One survivor changed the loop condition **`i <= offset + limit`** to **`i < offset + limit`**. That changes **how many items are returned**, yet **every test still passed**.

Coverage said "done"; mutation testing showed the tests barely checked the behaviour.

## 28. Cyclomatic complexity

Now from measuring **tests** to measuring **code**.

**Cyclomatic complexity** (Thomas **McCabe**, 1976) counts the **number of independent paths** through a piece of code.

- **By the graph:** draw the function as a **control-flow graph**, where each straight run of statements is a **node** and each jump is an **edge**. Then complexity = **E − N + 2**.
- **Shortcut:** **1 + the number of decision points**: +1 for each `if`, loop, `case`, and each `&&` / `||` in a condition.

| Code | Complexity |
|---|---|
| No branches | 1 |
| One `if` | 2 |
| A `switch` with 20 cases | 21 |

The common advice is to keep functions **at or below 10**. McCabe himself called 10 **reasonable but not magical**, and noted an exception: a function that is one big **`switch` over many independent cases**. A 20-case switch scores 21 yet is **easy to read**.

---

## 29. Cognitive complexity

**Cognitive complexity** (from **SonarSource**) measures **how hard code is to understand**, not how many paths it has.

- A **flat `switch`** adds very little: it's easy to read.
- **Nesting** adds more and more. An `if` inside a loop inside an `if` is much harder to hold in your head than three `if`s in a row.

| Code shape | Cyclomatic | Cognitive |
|---|---|---|
| Long, flat `switch` | **High** | **Low** |
| Three levels of nesting | Moderate | **High** |

**Demo (shown in the lesson):** two tools run on the same package.

- **Cyclomatic:** the hub's `Run` method scored **8**, third after two stream handlers.
- **Cognitive:** the same method scored **19**, jumping to the top alongside the WebSocket handler.
- **Reading the code itself:** it had **eight ways in** and was **deeply nested**, and genuinely hard to read.

**Lesson:** don't trust either number blindly or use it as a hard rule. Use the tools to **flag** code, look at **what they point to**, and **decide as a team**.

## 30. Linters, formatters, type checkers and static analysis

These tools find problems **without running the code**:

| Tool | What it does | What it doesn't do |
|---|---|---|
| **Linter** | Scans source for **suspicious patterns**: a condition that's **always true**, an **error that's never checked** | Not syntax (the compiler's job), not logical correctness (impossible to know without expected outputs) |
| **Formatter** | Rewrites code into a **standard layout** agreed by the team | Doesn't change behaviour |
| **Type checker** | Catches **type misuse**, e.g. arithmetic on a variable declared as a string. Built into languages like Go, TypeScript and Rust and shown in editors such as VS Code. | — |
| **Static analysis** | A more advanced linter: **follows values through the program** from a starting point and checks conditions along the way | — |

Examples: **ESLint** for TypeScript/JavaScript; for Go, `go vet` and the wider lint ecosystem.

**Code quality is subjective.** Beyond these tools there's no objective, deterministic way to decide whether code is "high quality". Linters and conventions help to a point.

## Key takeaways

- A **test** is a second program that runs your program and makes claims; a **runner** generates the entry point and collects results.
- The biggest value of tests is **catching regressions** in **CI**. Bad or flaky tests give **false confidence**.
- Classify tests by **what they may touch**: **small** (one process), **medium** (one machine), **large** (anything). **Leaving the process** is what makes tests slow and flaky.
- **Test doubles:** dummy, stub, spy, mock, fake. Prefer **state verification**; avoid **change-detector** tests.
- **Don't mock what you don't own.** Wrap third parties in your own interface, and check it with a few **sandbox contract tests**.
- Make code testable with **dependency injection** and a **functional core / imperative shell**.
- Use a **real database** (transaction per test, template databases, **Testcontainers**), **real HTTP** (`httptest`, MSW), and **conditions or injected clocks** instead of sleeps. Aim for **hermetic** tests.
- **TDD** = red → green → **refactor**. It fits when you know the answer but not the implementation.
- **Flaky tests:** mainly async waits, concurrency and order dependency. Delete or quarantine them.
- **Coverage** shows what **ran**, not what was **checked**. Read the uncovered lines; use **mutation testing** to test the tests.
- **Cyclomatic** (paths) and **cognitive** (readability) complexity are **flags**, not rules. Linters, formatters, type checkers and static analysis catch issues **without running code**.
